title.rendered: Shipping a Web App in 30 Days

content.rendered:
Thirty days sounds short until you scope it properly. Here is how we break a web application down so it actually ships, and what we deliberately leave for the second release.

Week one is decisions, not code

We spend the first week agreeing the scope, the data model, and the two or three screens that matter most. Everything else is written down as a later release. The goal is not to build less. The goal is to know exactly what done means before we open an editor.

Working software every week

You get a deployable build every Friday from week two onwards. No staging theatre, no big-bang reveal. If something is wrong, you see it on a real URL while there is still time to change it.

What we push to later

Settings screens nobody has asked for, edge cases around a feature you may not ship, and anything that depends on a decision you have not made. Cutting scope early is the single biggest reason our projects finish on time.

If it is not in the week-one scope list, it is not in this release.

Choosing the stack

We default to a modern React and TypeScript setup with a straightforward API layer, because it is fast to build with and easy for your next developer to pick up. We will argue for something else when the problem actually calls for it.

title.rendered: Offline-First Mobile Apps for Low-Connectivity Markets

content.rendered:
Most mobile app architecture assumes a reliable connection. In parts of Cameroon, that assumption quietly breaks your product. Offline-first is not a luxury feature when your users are in the field.

Assume the network is the exception

We design so that the local device is the source of truth and the server is a synchronisation target. Every write lands on the device first, is queued, and is retried when connectivity returns. The user experience never depends on a request finishing.

Conflict resolution has to be decided up front

The hard question is not offline, it is two people editing the same record while one of them is offline. We pick a strategy during week one, usually last-write-wins with an audit trail, and we tell you what we chose and why.

Make sync visible

A silent sync that sometimes fails is worse than an honest one. We show people when their work has been saved locally, when it is queued, and when it has actually reached the server.

Test it on a bad network, not a good one

Every release goes out on a throttled connection with packets dropped. If the app only works on office wifi, it does not work.

title.rendered: Where LLM Features Actually Help (And Where They Do Not)

content.rendered:
Most AI features we are asked for are a chatbot bolted onto a product nobody wanted. The ones that survive contact with real users tend to be much smaller and much more specific.

Good candidates

Summarising a long document a user already has. Turning messy free text into structured fields. Drafting something the user is going to edit anyway. Search that understands intent rather than keywords. These save the user typing and are easy to evaluate.

Bad candidates

Anything the user can do faster themselves with one click. Anything where a wrong answer is expensive and the user cannot tell it is wrong. Anything where the model is being asked to invent facts rather than reorganise information you gave it.

Design for the wrong answer

Show the source. Let people correct it. Make it obvious when the model is unsure. A feature that quietly returns nonsense destroys more trust than having no feature at all.

Measure the boring thing

Time to completion and correction rate tell you whether the feature works. Number of prompts does not. We instrument both before we ship.

title.rendered: Data Pipelines That People Actually Trust

content.rendered:
A dashboard nobody believes is worse than no dashboard. Trust in data is a design problem, and it is mostly won in the first ten minutes of someone opening the thing.

Show the data's age on everything

Every number carries a timestamp. If a figure is four hours stale, say so right next to it rather than in a footer nobody reads. Staleness you can see is a problem; staleness you have to guess about destroys confidence.

Make the pipeline visible

When something fails, the person looking at the dashboard should be able to see that it failed, when, and why, without opening a monitoring tool. A red row saying payment_events, failed 14:32, bad schema beats a support ticket.

Reconcile against something a human trusts

Pick one number the business already reconciles manually, and match it weekly. If your pipeline and their spreadsheet agree, you have earned the right to show them the other forty numbers.

Idempotency is not optional

Jobs will retry. Networks will drop. Write every step so running it twice is safe, or your totals will drift and you will spend a week explaining a number nobody can reproduce.

title.rendered: What a Good Product Design Review Actually Catches

content.rendered:
A design review is not a meeting about whether people like the colours. Done properly it catches the expensive mistakes while they are still cheap to fix.

It catches the thing you cannot un-send

Once a user has seen a flow, changing it costs you. Reviews exist to change the flow before anyone depends on it, which is why we run them in week one rather than the last week.

It catches inconsistent states

Loading, empty, error, and permission-denied are where most products quietly break. A review that only looks at the happy path has not really reviewed anything.

It catches the assumption nobody stated

Someone decided the user knows what a workspace is. Nobody wrote that down, so nobody questioned it. Reviews are largely the act of making hidden assumptions visible and then arguing about them.

What it is not

It is not a vote. It is not a place to relitigate the brief. And it is not the moment to add a feature, because a feature added in review is a feature nobody scoped, costed, or tested.

title.rendered: Why We Hand Over the Code, the Repo, and the Keys

content.rendered:
The test of a software project is not whether the demo went well. It is what happens on the day we stop being involved.

You should be able to replace us

If a project cannot survive its original authors leaving, it was never finished. We make sure your team can run, deploy, debug, and extend the codebase without calling us, and we prove it by walking your people through it before we hand over.

Documentation that matches reality

A README written last week describing a system that changed on Tuesday is worse than none, because it is trusted. We write documentation against what is actually deployed, and we update it as part of the work rather than as a separate task at the end.

No hostage architecture

We do not build things that only work through us. If your project depends on a proprietary framework we wrote and only we understand, you do not own it. You rented it.

Everything we build lives in your repository, under your accounts, with your domain.

What we keep

We are happy to keep maintaining it, on a retainer you can end. The difference is that you never have to.
